To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Intel Pentium 3 and 4 processors provide an extremely efficient covert channel, which can be used to transfer data between threads at speeds of up to 2.4 GB/s, and that the same processor provides a means of monitoring the execution of other threads, allowing in some cases for the theft of cryptographic keys.

1) the sharing of processor caches between multiple execution threads provides a high bandwidth covert channel that can be used for the theft of cryptographic keys, and 2) this covert channel can be used to steal cryptographic keys even when the malicious thread has no access to the memory locations that contain the key.

a malicious thread on a Hyper-Threading processor can: (1) monitor the execution of other threads on the processor, and (2) steal cryptographic keys from the other threads, if they are used to encrypt or decrypt data.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question: can a malicious thread steal the cryptographic keys used by another thread?
We have been unable to find any prior research that has considered the security implications of the simultaneous multithreading of a superscalar microprocessor.
the question of whether or not the execution resources of the processor should be shared, and the answer we give to that question is “No, not unless the sharing is done in a very careful way.
the following question: “How much do I trust my processor?”
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
“Hyper-Threading is not a good idea.”
the use of Hyper-Threading in a cryptographic system can be dangerous.
“Hyper-Threading is a security disaster.”
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the sharing of execution resources between threads in modern processors is a double-edged sword, which can be used both to improve performance and to facilitate attacks.
a malicious thread can steal the cryptographic key of another thread by monitoring its memory accesses.
the security of cryptographic software should be evaluated in the context of the entire computer system, not just the application itself.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sharing of processor execution resources between threads, even at the cache level, can be a security risk.
, in order for a processor designer to prevent the use of a cache as a covert channel, the caches must not be shared.
the design of modern processors is not as simple as it might first appear.
